title: Copilot or ChatGPT Enterprise: which is right for your UK business?
excerpt: A UK buyer's guide to Microsoft 365 Copilot vs ChatGPT Enterprise: sterling pricing, UK data residency, integration depth, and which one fits a UK business already committed to Microsoft 365 versus one that isn't.
content:
For most UK organisations already running Microsoft 365, Microsoft 365 Copilot is the practical default. It costs £30 per user per month as an add-on and works inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams from day one. ChatGPT Enterprise costs more to negotiate, publishes no fixed price, and suits teams that want a model-agnostic assistant with UK and EU data residency built in.

What do Microsoft 365 Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise actually do?

Both are AI assistants built on frontier large language models, sold to organisations rather than individuals. Past that, they solve slightly different problems, and the "vs" in most buyer's-guide headlines hides how different the actual buying decision is.

Microsoft is selling an upgrade to software you probably already own. OpenAI is selling a platform you have to decide to adopt from scratch. That difference shapes almost everything else in this comparison, from the sticker price to the change-management effort.

Microsoft 365 Copilot lives inside the apps a UK office already runs on. It drafts in Word, builds formulas in Excel, summarises threads in Outlook, and takes notes in Teams meetings. Its whole pitch is that staff never leave the tools they already know.

ChatGPT Enterprise is the business-grade version of the assistant most UK staff have already used at home. It's a standalone chat and API platform, not bolted to a specific office suite, with enterprise-grade security, admin controls and usage analytics layered on top.

Picture a UK marketing agency and a UK accountancy practice side by side. The agency already lives in Google Workspace and a scattered set of design tools, so a Microsoft-only assistant would be one more login for something that doesn't touch its daily workflow. The accountancy practice runs Outlook, Excel and SharePoint for everything, so Copilot slots straight into work that already exists.

The fence-sitters here (a lot of UK IT teams right now) tend to frame this as "which is the better AI." That's the wrong question. The right one is whether your organisation's AI problem is "help my existing tools" or "give my team a general-purpose assistant."

How much do they cost a UK business in 2026?

Microsoft prices Copilot as an add-on licence, not a standalone product, which changes the real bill more than the headline number suggests.

OpenAI runs the opposite model for ChatGPT Business and Enterprise: no underlying office suite to buy, but Enterprise pricing itself is opaque by design, negotiated seat by seat.

Dimension Microsoft 365 Copilot ChatGPT Business ChatGPT Enterprise
List price £30/user/month add-on (enterprise), $21/user/month for the Business SKU (up to 300 seats) $20/user/month annual, $25 monthly (cut from $25/$30 on 2 April 2026) Not published. Quote-only, negotiated per contract
Prerequisite spend Requires a qualifying Microsoft 365 plan (Business Standard, Business Premium, E3 or E5) None. Standalone None. Standalone
Seat minimum None published for the enterprise add-on 2 seats None published, though smaller organisations often get quoted for more seats than they need
Best for Teams already committed to Microsoft 365 who want AI inside Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams Small teams wanting a straightforward, cheap ChatGPT seat with admin controls Larger organisations wanting model-agnostic AI, UK/EU data residency and enterprise governance
Pricing last checked September 2026 September 2026 September 2026

Read that "prerequisite spend" row carefully. A UK business with no Microsoft 365 estate at all is not comparing £30 against $20. It's comparing £30 plus a Business Premium or E3 licence (typically £15 to £45 per user per month on its own) against a single ChatGPT Business seat. The office-suite bill is the part most cost comparisons leave out.

Run the numbers for a 50-seat UK professional services firm already paying for Microsoft 365 Business Premium. Adding Copilot at £30 a head comes to £1,500 a month, on top of the licence it already holds.

The same 50 seats on ChatGPT Business at $20 a head (around £16 at September 2026 exchange rates, Tom & Co conversion) comes to roughly £800 a month, with no prerequisite spend at all. The gap narrows considerably once you count the Microsoft 365 licence the firm was already paying for.

Billing terms matter almost as much as the headline rate. Both vendors charge a premium for monthly billing over an annual commitment, so a UK finance team modelling a multi-year rollout should compare like for like, annual against annual, before either number goes into a board paper.

Large language models were the most widely used AI technology among UK businesses with 10 or more employees in June 2026, ahead of image and data-processing AI tools, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Applying that 18% adoption figure to the Department for Business and Trade's 2024 business population estimates (roughly 257,000 UK businesses with 10 or more staff) puts around 46,000 UK businesses already running a large language model day to day (Tom & Co analysis combining the two datasets). Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise are both fighting for a slice of that same 46,000.

Which one wins on embedding AI into daily work?

Copilot's advantage is structural, not clever prompting. If your team's day already runs through Outlook, Excel and Teams, Copilot shows up where the work already happens rather than asking anyone to open a new tab.

ChatGPT Enterprise's advantage runs the other way. It doesn't care which office suite, CRM or design tool you use, so it fits organisations running Google Workspace, a mixed stack, or no single dominant suite at all. Its GPTs and custom actions can connect to internal tools without Microsoft as the go-between.

Raw model quality is closer than the marketing suggests. Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise both sit on frontier-class models that trade places on benchmark leaderboards month to month, and our own comparison of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for UK businesses covers that ground in detail. For this decision, workflow fit matters more than a few benchmark points either way.

Integration depth is starting to converge, too. OpenAI has adopted the Model Context Protocol across its products, and Microsoft has added MCP support to Copilot Studio, so both platforms are moving towards the same open standard for connecting an assistant to your own systems rather than staying locked to their own connector catalogues.

The honest read for most UK teams: if you're already deep in Microsoft 365, Copilot's head start inside the apps is hard to give up for a marginal capability gain elsewhere. If you're not, that head start doesn't exist and the decision comes down to the sections below.

Which one wins on UK data protection and security?

This is where the two genuinely differ, and where a UK compliance team should spend its diligence time rather than on the pricing table.

Data residency

Microsoft 365 Copilot keeps prompts, retrieved content and responses inside the customer's own Microsoft 365 tenant boundary, stored at rest in the tenant's provisioned region (UK South and UK West for UK tenants). OpenAI now offers the equivalent for ChatGPT Enterprise: in-region data residency, including a UK option, for approved advanced data controls customers.

Training on your data

Neither platform trains its foundation models on business customers' prompts or documents by default. The ICO's own privacy notice for its Microsoft 365 Copilot use states that its Copilot data stays inside its secure UK Microsoft 365 and Azure tenancy and is not used to train foundation models, a position OpenAI mirrors for ChatGPT Enterprise and Business customers.

Guidance for staff

The National Cyber Security Centre's guidance on AI and cyber security is blunt on this point: classify your data before you decide what can go into any AI tool, Copilot or ChatGPT included, rather than relying on the vendor's contract terms alone. That's a governance job, not a procurement one.

Neither vendor's admin console does that classification work for you. Both give an IT admin the switches to block sensitive categories, restrict connectors, and review usage logs, but someone in the organisation still has to decide what counts as sensitive before those switches mean anything.

Neither product removes the need for a DPIA on a new AI use case. Our guide to the ICO's AI and UK GDPR expectations covers what that assessment actually needs to show.

A UK financial services or law firm carries an extra layer on top of both: sector guidance from the FCA or SRA on how client data can be used with any third-party AI tool. Data residency answers where the data sits, not whether a given client matter is allowed near either tool at all, and that second question sits with your own regulator.

Which one is right for your organisation?

Match the decision to your starting point, not to which product got the better headline this quarter.

Factor in switching cost before you sign anything. Copilot's advantage compounds the longer a team uses it, because prompts, custom instructions and Teams-specific habits build up inside the Microsoft ecosystem. ChatGPT Enterprise's advantage compounds differently, through custom GPTs, API integrations and internal tooling that don't care which model sits behind them. Neither is free to unwind once a team is a year into using it, so the 30-day pilot below matters more than the price on the page.

A UK professional services firm on Microsoft 365 Business Premium, wanting AI drafting inside Word and Outlook with minimal change management, should default to Copilot. The adoption curve is shorter because nothing about the interface changes.

A UK scale-up running Google Workspace, a bespoke tech stack, or planning to build custom internal tools on top of an assistant, gets more from ChatGPT Enterprise's model-agnostic approach and its API access, even before data residency and governance controls enter the comparison.

A larger UK organisation already committed to both Microsoft 365 and a separate AI programme sometimes runs both, Copilot for the day-to-day office work, ChatGPT Enterprise for a specific build or research team that needs a different toolset. That's not indecision, it's matching the tool to the job twice over.

A regulated UK firm, whether that's a law firm bound by SRA rules or a lender working to FCA expectations, should treat the vendor choice as the second decision, not the first. The first is whether a given piece of client or customer data is allowed anywhere near a third-party AI tool at all, whichever badge is on the login screen.

What should a UK IT leader do this quarter?

  1. Map your actual base cost. Add your existing (or required) Microsoft 365 licence tier to the Copilot add-on before comparing it against ChatGPT's standalone price.
  2. Ask both vendors for a UK data residency confirmation in writing. Verbal assurances from a sales call are not a data processing agreement.
  3. Run a DPIA before either rollout, not after. Our ICO and AI GDPR guide sets out the questions it needs to answer.
  4. Pilot with one team for 30 days before an organisation-wide licence commitment on either platform.
  5. Revisit the comparison every two quarters. Pricing, seat minimums and data residency options on both sides have moved multiple times in 2026 alone.
